Q: Am I thinking in right direction about busy waiting and blocking I/O A:

If a server is coded with blocking style I/O, if there are multiple users are connected to it and if one user asks for I/O then whole server will stop.

The definition and/or implementation of this "server" needs to be defined/clarified.

BTW "stop" is a poor word choice here; it has a connotation of finality and/or termination. "Pause" or "suspend" is a better description of what blocking does to the executing thread.

If i am considering that server code is single threaded and if i am using busy waiting then it may waste CPU cycle but it wont make whole server stop as it will be preempted by scheduler of process by OS of server.

That sentence ends with four prepositional phrases, but the last three adds confusion rather than clarity.

Seems like you're asking if blocking I/O is bad, and busy waiting for I/O completion is benign if not a better alternative.

In a modern multitasking (or mulithreading) operating system, system calls typically default to blocking mode. That is, return to the calling process/thread occurs after the system request is deemed complete. In the meantime the calling process/thread is suspended (rather than "stopped"). This facilitates concurrent execution of other (waiting) processes/threads, and increases CPU efficiency and processing throughput.

If the system call has a non-blocking variant, then return to the calling process/thread occurs as soon as possible and (probably) before completion of the request/operation. Additional system calls typically have to be made to determine the completion status.

The availability of non-blocking system calls is to facilitate an (old) technique to enhance processing throughput with a single process/thread known as asynchronous I/O or asynch I/O. Such an asynch operation/system-call will be non-blocking, and allow the process to perform some useful processing concurrent with the I/O operation. However modern OSes and programming languages typically support multi-threading, which typically leads to more-maintainable source code.

In other words, when a blocking syscall is not used, a well-written process/thread should perform useful work after making the non-blocking system call. A poorly-written program employs sleeping and polling to wait for completion instead of using the built-in event-driven efficiency of a blocking syscall. A badly-written program employs busy waiting for completion, and steals CPU time from other waiting processes/threads. Busy waiting is an inferior I/O technique that can only be tolerated and justified in rather limited situations because it is simply detrimental to overall system throughput.

Q: How can I list only files and not directories of a directory in Bash? A: 
ls -p | grep -v /

ls -p lets you show / after the folder name, which acts as a tag for you to remove.
